rv.q: Mamet's all-too-human creations may be talking about black and white, but these all-too-human people are dealing with a hot-button subject in various incendiary shades of gray.
Mamet has fashioned a theatrical thriller that keeps you guessing about the motivations and machinations of everyone onstage.
Race is wholly watchable. Gripping, actually. Don't believe anyone who argues otherwise.
Mamet's latest play is a provocative examination of racial attitudes that doesn't quite live up to its inflammatory promise, despite strong performances from the cast.
Mr. Izzard’s performance is smart and sensitive, but it generally feels more submissive than subversive.
But as it is, it's a lit fuse that crackles and pops but never quite explodes.
He makes the ineffable all too effable, and eff you if you can’t take it.
The more troubling question is whether, ultimately, we end up caring what he thinks in "Race," the attractively cast, surprisingly stale new play...
Audiences might expect this type of awkwardly constructed, flailing acrimony from a 15-year-old with a Twitter account, not from a Pulitzer Prize winner.
Mamet's treatment may be far from bright, but the light it shines on this ever-contentious issue is enough to make it one of the most illuminating and invigorating plays of 2009.
And Mamet deserves credit for a briskly entertaining, if flawed, study.
Played fast, under the author's direction, its 80 or so minutes feel like a speedy round of post-Shavian ping-pong.
There's no denying the production under Mamet's direction is plenty entertaining and thought provoking.
The arguments feel like moves on a game board, not words from the heart.
Slick but hollow, 'Race' entertains as it unfolds, but grows increasingly wobbly as it twists its way to an unsatisfying wrap-up.
